| where delay_sec >= 0 AND delay_sec <= 30
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as procTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name="php-fpm.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="php-cgi.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="httpd.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="w3wp.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="nginx.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="apache2" OR Processes.parent_process_name="httpd" OR Processes.parent_process_name="php-fpm") (Processes.process_name="cmd.exe" OR Processes.process_name="powershell.exe" OR Processes.process_name="pwsh.exe" OR Processes.process_name="sh" OR Processes.process_name="bash" OR Processes.process_name="nc.exe" OR Processes.process_name="whoami.exe" OR Processes.process_name="net.exe" OR Processes.process_name="wscript.exe" OR Processes.process_name="cscript.exe") by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.process_id
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| join type=inner dest [
    | tstats summariesonly=false min(_time) as fileTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action=created (Filesystem.file_path="*/writable/uploads/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\writable\\uploads\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/public/uploads/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\public\\uploads\\*") by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name
    | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
    | where match(file_name, "(?i)\.(php|phtml|phar)$")
  ]
| eval delay_sec = procTime - fileTime
| where delay_sec >= 0 AND delay_sec <= 30
Direct HTTP GET to PHP file inside CodeIgniter4 uploads directory AIActions on Objectives High
Detects web traffic invoking a .php file that lives under writable/uploads or public/uploads — the post-exploit shell access vector for CVE-2026-48062. Legitimate CI4 apps NEVER serve PHP from these directories; any GET to them is high-fidelity web-shell signal. Rationale: Article workflow: shell.php is uploaded under writable/uploads, then 'allow PHP or other executable files to run from that directory' leads to ACE. The next attacker step is an HTTP request to that file. CodeIgniter4 docs explicitly recommend `writable/uploads` as the canonical upload path — making this directory + .php pairing entirely abnormal in healthy CI4 deployments. Cross-checked against: • https://codeigniter.com/user_guide/libraries/uploaded_files.html#moving-files • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2gr4-ppc7-7mhx
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate CodeIgniter4 modules that intentionally route through /uploads/ (very rare, itself a misconfiguration)
  • 404 probe noise from scanners (filterable on scStatus 404)
  • Pen-test engagement against the patched application
  • Asset discovery scanners (Nuclei, Burp) authorized by IT
  • Developer manually testing the upload feature in production
Suppression filter
| where scStatus != 404 and cIP !in ("<approved_scanner_ip>", "<security_team_ip>")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Check scStatus — 200 means the shell answered, 404 means nothing landed. Pull the cIP and check whether it matches the source IP of the upload POST that preceded it. Identify the csUriStem filename and pivot to DeviceFileEvents to confirm the file exists on disk and review its contents (polyglot check). Step 2 (contain): Block cIP at the WAF/firewall, delete the .php from disk, take the affected CI4 app offline if scStatus 200 (confirmed RCE), preserve web logs and the file. If still vulnerable, force-upgrade CI4 to 4.7.3+. Step 3 (hunt): Pull every csUriStem the cIP hit in the last 14 days — look for other web shells the actor planted. Pivot on csUserAgent for matching scans against other CI4 hosts. Search DeviceProcessEvents for any cmd/sh spawned by the web server in the 5 minutes around the scStatus 200 hit.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| where RemoteUrl matches regex @"(?i)/(writable|public)/?uploads?/[^/]+\.(php|phtml|phar|php5|php7)([\?]|$)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, LocalIP, LocalPort
| order by Timestamp desc
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod in ("GET", "POST")
| where csUriStem matches regex @"(?i)/(writable|public)/?uploads?/[^/]+\.(php|phtml|phar|php5|php7)$"
| project TimeGenerated, sSiteName, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent, csUserName, TimeTaken
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Nx s1ngularity 'telemetry.js' postinstall payload execution AIExploitation High
Detects execution of the telemetry.js postinstall script associated with the Nx s1ngularity npm supply-chain compromise (Aug 2025). The script is invoked by npm during install, scrapes GitHub/npm tokens, SSH keys and crypto wallets, and exfiltrates them to attacker-created public GitHub repos. Rationale: Anchored on the article-named 'telemetry.js' postinstall script and 's1ngularity' brand string. Cross-checked at the Nx post-mortem (nx.dev/blog/s1ngularity-postmortem) and Datadog Security Labs which both confirm telemetry.js as the canonical Nx-poisoned filename invoked from package.json's postinstall hook. Parent-filename narrowing to JS package managers removes the obvious FP shape. Cross-checked against: • https://nx.dev/blog/s1ngularity-postmortem • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/learnings-from-recent-npm-compromises/ • https://snyk.io/blog/weaponizing-ai-coding-agents-for-malware-in-the-nx-malicious-package/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Nx packages published before/after the malicious window — current versions of @nx/* may still ship a benign telemetry.js
  • Developer hand-running 'node scripts/telemetry.js' in a non-Nx repo unrelated to npm install
  • Internal monorepo with a homegrown telemetry.js used in pre/post hooks
  • CI runners that pin to a known-clean Nx version but still surface the filename
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "telemetry.js" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("\\node_modules\\@nrwl\\nx\\","\\node_modules\\nx\\") and SHA256 in ("<known-good-nx-sha256>"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull the full ProcessCreate row + parent cmdline; confirm the parent is an active 'npm install' or 'yarn add' invocation and not a manual 'node telemetry.js' run. Pivot DeviceFileEvents for SHA256 of the telemetry.js file under node_modules. 2) CONTAIN: isolate the device via Defender Live Response, revoke the user's GitHub PAT, npm token, and any AWS keys from ~/.aws/credentials, and rotate SSH keys touched on that host. 3) HUNT: search for outbound connections to api.github.com creating 's1ngularity-repository*' under the user's GH account, query DeviceFileEvents for 'results.b64' across the fleet, and review npm audit log for which package version dragged it in.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe","npx.cmd","yarn.cmd","yarn.exe","pnpm.cmd","pnpm.exe","bun.exe")
    or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "telemetry.js" or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("s1ngularity","@nrwl/nx","nx-cloud")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe","npx.cmd","yarn.cmd","pnpm.cmd","bun.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "telemetry.js" or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("s1ngularity","@nrwl/nx","nx-cloud")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^(node\.exe|npm\.(cmd|exe)|npx\.cmd|yarn\.(cmd|exe)|pnpm\.(cmd|exe)|bun\.exe)$/i CommandLine=/telemetry\.js|s1ngularity/i

TruffleHog secret scanner spawned by Node/npm (Shai-Hulud worm pattern) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the TruffleHog secret-scanning binary being launched as a child of node/npm/yarn/pnpm/bun. The Shai-Hulud worm installs the Bun runtime mid-install and uses TruffleHog to scrape API keys, tokens, and cloud credentials from the host before pushing them to a hardcoded webhook. Rationale: Article explicitly names TruffleHog as the Shai-Hulud credential-harvest tool. Sysdig and ReversingLabs both confirm trufflehog is fetched + executed under npm install context. Pairing the binary signal with a JS-package-manager parent eliminates the legit dev/CI TruffleHog runs (which are launched from CI YAML or the user shell, not from node). Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/shai-hulud-the-novel-self-replicating-worm-infecting-hundreds-of-npm-packages • https://www.reversinglabs.com/blog/shai-hulud-worm-npm • https://checkmarx.com/zero-post/inside-shai-huluds-maw-how-the-npm-worm-exploits-and-propagates/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Pre-commit hook calling 'npx trufflehog' as legitimate secret scanning (common in modern dev workflows)
  • GitHub Actions self-hosted runner with the trufflehog action where the workflow shell parent is node
  • CI orchestrator that wraps trufflehog in a node-based runner like 'turbo run'
  • Security researcher hand-running 'npx trufflehog filesystem .' against a repo
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pre-commit","husky","lint-staged") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("git-secrets","pre-commit"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull TruffleHog cmdline — Shai-Hulud invokes with '--json' and filesystem/git scopes targeting $HOME and common cred dirs. Check whether the parent chain includes an in-flight 'npm install' / 'npm ci' (vs an explicit user-typed npx). Sample the calling node process's argv. 2) CONTAIN: isolate the host, revoke all GitHub/npm/AWS/GCP tokens held by the user, and rotate any SSH keys present. Pull node_modules/<suspect-package> for IR. 3) HUNT: search for outbound to webhook.site (see Shai-Hulud beacon UC), look for new public GitHub repos under the user's account, query DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound to bun.sh and github.com/oven-sh/bun, and pivot on the SHA256 of the trufflehog binary across the fleet.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has "trufflehog" or ProcessCommandLine has "trufflehog"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe","npx.cmd","yarn.cmd","yarn.exe","pnpm.cmd","pnpm.exe","bun.exe","sh.exe","bash.exe")
    or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe","yarn.cmd","pnpm.cmd","bun.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "trufflehog" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "trufflehog"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe","npx.cmd","yarn.cmd","pnpm.cmd","bun.exe","sh","bash")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^(node\.exe|npm\.(cmd|exe)|npx\.cmd|yarn\.(cmd|exe)|pnpm\.(cmd|exe)|bun\.exe)$/i (ImageFileName=/trufflehog/i OR CommandLine=/trufflehog/i)

Nx s1ngularity exfil: GitHub repo 's1ngularity-repository' / 'results.b64' AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the Nx s1ngularity exfiltration pattern where the postinstall payload creates a public GitHub repository (s1ngularity-repository, sometimes numerically suffixed) under the victim's own account and commits a triple-base64-encoded credential bundle named results.b64. Surfaced via gh CLI, git, curl, or wget commandlines. Rationale: Anchored on two literal Nx s1ngularity strings ('s1ngularity-repository' and 'results.b64') corroborated by the Nx post-mortem, Datadog Security Labs, and CyberSecureFox. These strings are essentially unique — neither has a benign use. Multi-source detection (process + file) catches both the gh/git invocation and the staged bundle file. Cross-checked against: • https://nx.dev/blog/s1ngularity-postmortem • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/learnings-from-recent-npm-compromises/ • https://cybersecurefox.com/en/nx-supply-chain-attack-s1ngularity-github-actions-npm/
ATT&CKT1567.001 T1567
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal red-team replicating the IR scenario in a lab
  • Security researcher cloning the public s1ngularity-response repo (BunsDev/s1ngularity-response) for analysis — git clone URL would mention it
  • Threat-intel feed enrichment script that posts the literal string in a benign context
  • Incident response document containing the IOC strings opened in a script editor
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: capture the full cmdline + parent chain. Identify which GitHub account was authenticated via 'gh auth status' on the host. List public repos under that account ('gh repo list --visibility public') and check for s1ngularity-repository, s1ngularity-repository-0, ...-1, etc. 2) CONTAIN: delete the attacker-created public repos immediately (they expose credentials publicly). Revoke the GitHub PAT and all OAuth grants on that account, rotate npm/AWS/GCP keys, force-rotate SSH keypairs. Isolate the host. 3) HUNT: pivot on the user's other endpoints, search EmailEvents for any phishing that compromised the GitHub credential, and check DeviceFileEvents for ~/.gitconfig / ~/.npmrc tampering. Block 's1ngularity-repository*' as a regex in egress DLP.
union
(
    DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName in~ ("gh.exe","git.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("s1ngularity-repository","results.b64")
        or (ProcessCommandLine has "repo create" and ProcessCommandLine has "--public" and ProcessCommandLine has "s1ngularity")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
              ActionType = "ProcessCreated",
              Evidence = strcat(FileName, " :: ", ProcessCommandLine),
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
),
(
    DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName =~ "results.b64" or FolderPath has "s1ngularity-repository"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName,
              AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName,
              ActionType,
              Evidence = strcat(FolderPath, "\\", FileName),
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
)
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(
    SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where NewProcessName has_any ("gh.exe","git.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
    | where CommandLine has_any ("s1ngularity-repository","results.b64")
        or (CommandLine has "repo create" and CommandLine has "--public" and CommandLine has "s1ngularity")
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, Source="4688", Evidence = CommandLine, Parent = ParentProcessName
),
(
    ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where TargetFileName =~ "results.b64" or TargetFilePath has "s1ngularity-repository"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer = DvcHostname, Account = ActorUsername, Source="File", Evidence = TargetFilePath, Parent = ActingProcessName
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Shai-Hulud Webhook.site C2 beacon from Node/npm/Bun process AICommand & Control High
Detects outbound traffic to webhook.site, and specifically to the Shai-Hulud-attributed bundle path bb8ca5f6-4175-45d2-b042-fc9ebb8170b7, originating from a node/npm/yarn/pnpm/bun-spawned process. webhook.site is a free request-bin service that Shai-Hulud hardcodes as its credential dropbox. Rationale: webhook.site is a confirmed hardcoded Shai-Hulud C2 endpoint per Sysdig and Checkmarx (the bb8ca5f6 token is the literal bundle ID published in their write-ups). Tagging only npm-ecosystem-spawned connections cuts the legitimate developer-testing FP volume. The ShaiHuludMarker column lets the SOC promote any hit with the literal bundle ID straight to incident. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/shai-hulud-the-novel-self-replicating-worm-infecting-hundreds-of-npm-packages • https://checkmarx.com/zero-post/inside-shai-huluds-maw-how-the-npm-worm-exploits-and-propagates/ • https://www.reversinglabs.com/blog/shai-hulud-worm-npm
ATT&CKT1567 T1071.001 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer testing a Stripe/Twilio/Slack webhook by curling webhook.site from a node script during local dev
  • CI pipeline using webhook.site as a request bin for integration tests
  • Postman or Insomnia desktop client (electron/node-based) hitting webhook.site
  • QA engineer running 'npm test' against a service that sends webhooks for verification
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("test","integration","e2e","jest","mocha","playwright") and not (RemoteUrl has "bb8ca5f6-4175-45d2-b042-fc9ebb8170b7"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: confirm whether the URL path contains 'bb8ca5f6-4175-45d2-b042-fc9ebb8170b7' (ShaiHuludMarker=TRUE = treat as confirmed). For non-marker hits, pull the parent npm install context — was a package being installed when the connection fired? 2) CONTAIN: isolate host, block webhook.site at the proxy/DNS for npm-ecosystem User-Agents, force-revoke all GitHub PAT / npm tokens / cloud creds on the host. 3) HUNT: hash any node_modules subdir modified in the prior 24h, search for TruffleHog spawn (see related UC), look for s1ngularity-repository creation, and pivot on the SHA256 of the bun binary if present. Add the bb8ca5f6 path to TI feed and the DLP egress block list.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "webhook.site"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe","npx.cmd","yarn.cmd","yarn.exe","pnpm.cmd","pnpm.exe","bun.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
    or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe","yarn.cmd","pnpm.cmd","bun.exe")
| extend ShaiHuludMarker = iff(RemoteUrl has "bb8ca5f6-4175-45d2-b042-fc9ebb8170b7", "TRUE", "FALSE")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName,
          AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          RemoteUrl, ShaiHuludMarker, RemoteIP, RemotePort,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by ShaiHuludMarker desc, Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(
    ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DstHostname has "webhook.site" or Url has "webhook.site"
    | extend ShaiHuludMarker = iff(Url has "bb8ca5f6-4175-45d2-b042-fc9ebb8170b7", "TRUE", "FALSE")
    | project TimeGenerated, Source="NetworkSession", Host=DvcHostname, SrcUser=SrcUsername, Dst=DstHostname, Url, ShaiHuludMarker
),
(
    DnsEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where Name =~ "webhook.site" or Name endswith ".webhook.site"
    | project TimeGenerated, Source="DNS", Host=Computer, SrcUser="", Dst=Name, Url="", ShaiHuludMarker="DNS-only"
)
| order by ShaiHuludMarker desc, TimeGenerated desc
title: Shai-Hulud Webhook.site Beacon from Node/npm Process
id: 8c4f1a2d-7e5b-4f3c-9a8d-2b1c3d4e5f6a
description: Detects outbound network connection to webhook.site from a node/npm/yarn/pnpm/bun-spawned process, the hardcoded C2 dropbox used by the Shai-Hulud npm worm
references:
    - https://www.aikido.dev/blog/npm-v12-block-postinstall
    - https://www.sysdig.com/blog/shai-hulud-the-novel-self-replicating-worm-infecting-hundreds-of-npm-packages
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/19
tags:
    - attack.command_and_control
    - attack.t1071.001
    - attack.t1567

Bun runtime fetched mid-npm-install (Shai-Hulud / Mini Shai-Hulud staging) AIDelivery Medium
Detects npm/node/yarn/pnpm pulling and installing the Bun JavaScript runtime during a package install. Both Shai-Hulud (Nov 2025) and Mini Shai-Hulud (May 2026) stage the cred-stealer payload inside Bun, so an npm install that drags in Bun on a host that previously never ran it is a strong supply-chain marker. Rationale: Article explicitly says Shai-Hulud 'installed the Bun runtime during setup' and Mini Shai-Hulud 'planted a preinstall hook that pulled the Bun runtime'. The two URL signals (bun.sh/install and github.com/oven-sh/bun) are how Bun's documented installer fetches. Pairing with a node/npm parent eliminates the legitimate dev-who-runs-curl-from-shell FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/shai-hulud-the-novel-self-replicating-worm-infecting-hundreds-of-npm-packages • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
ATT&CKT1105 T1195.002 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer or CI runner that genuinely uses Bun as a runtime and runs the official installer from a node-wrapped task
  • Devcontainer post-create script that node-bootstraps Bun on container build
  • Polyglot monorepo where one workspace runs 'npm run setup' that contains 'curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | bash'
  • Engineer evaluating Bun as a replacement runtime and triggering installer from a node script
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName in (dynamic(["<known-bun-dev-hosts>"])) or AccountName in (dynamic(["<known-bun-developers>"])))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: was Bun already present on this host before this event? Query DeviceInfo / DeviceFileEvents for prior bun.exe sightings on this DeviceId. If first-seen on host AND during an npm install, treat as suspect. 2) CONTAIN: stop the npm install, isolate the host, pull node_modules for IR snapshot. Revoke tokens the host had access to. 3) HUNT: check the same time window for TruffleHog spawn, webhook.site beacons, and s1ngularity-repository creation under the user's GitHub. Pivot per-host: a new bun.exe SHA256 appearing on N hosts within hours = worm propagation.
let JsPkgMgr = dynamic(["node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe","npx.cmd","yarn.cmd","yarn.exe","pnpm.cmd","pnpm.exe"]);
let BunSignals = dynamic(["bun.sh/install","oven-sh/bun","install.sh"]);
union
(
    DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (JsPkgMgr)
        or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ (JsPkgMgr)
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any (BunSignals) or FileName in~ ("bun.exe","bun")
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
              Source = "Process",
              Evidence = strcat(FileName, " :: ", ProcessCommandLine),
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
),
(
    DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any ("bun.sh/install","oven-sh/bun")
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (JsPkgMgr) or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
        or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ (JsPkgMgr)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName,
              AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName,
              Source = "Network",
              Evidence = RemoteUrl,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
)
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe","npx.cmd","yarn.cmd","pnpm.cmd")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("bun.sh/install","oven-sh/bun")
    or (ActingProcessCommandLine has "curl" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "install.sh" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "bun")
    or ActingProcessName endswith "bun.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Bun Runtime Download Triggered During npm Install
id: 1a2b3c4d-5e6f-7a8b-9c0d-1e2f3a4b5c6d
description: Detects download or first-time execution of the Bun JavaScript runtime triggered by npm/node/yarn/pnpm, consistent with the Shai-Hulud and Mini Shai-Hulud npm worms which pull Bun mid-install to run a credential stealer
references:
    - https://www.aikido.dev/blog/npm-v12-block-postinstall
    - https://www.sysdig.com/blog/shai-hulud-the-novel-self-replicating-worm-infecting-hundreds-of-npm-packages
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/19
tags:
    - attack.execution
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1105
    - attack.t1195.002
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\\node.exe'
            - '\\npm.cmd'
            - '\\npm.exe'

level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\node.exe OR *\\NODE.EXE OR *\\npm.exe OR *\\NPM.EXE OR *\\npm.cmd OR *\\yarn.cmd OR *\\pnpm.cmd) (@CommandLine:*bun.sh/install* OR @CommandLine:*oven-sh/bun* OR @Image:*\\bun.exe OR @Image:*\\BUN.EXE)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^(node\.exe|npm\.(cmd|exe)|npx\.cmd|yarn\.(cmd|exe)|pnpm\.(cmd|exe))$/i (CommandLine=/bun\.sh\/install|oven-sh\/bun/i OR ImageFileName=/bun\.exe$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node.exe","npm.exe","npm.cmd","npx.cmd","yarn.exe","yarn.cmd","pnpm.exe","pnpm.cmd","node","npm","yarn","pnpm")) AND (Processes.process="*bun.sh/install*" OR Processes.process="*oven-sh/bun*" OR (Processes.process="*curl*" AND Processes.process="*install.sh*" AND Processes.process="*bun*") OR Processes.process_name IN ("bun.exe","bun")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

Implicit node-gyp rebuild from binding.gyp during npm install AIExploitation Medium
Hunt-tier surface for the binding.gyp attack path that npm v12 closes — packages that ship a binding.gyp trigger an implicit 'node-gyp rebuild' during npm install with no script declared in package.json, executing arbitrary build code. Hunt for node-gyp invocations spawned by npm/yarn/pnpm and baseline against your approved native-module set. Rationale: The article calls out the binding.gyp attack vector explicitly: 'When a package ships a binding.gyp, npm runs an implicit node-gyp rebuild for it during install, so a dependency with a spotless package.json can still execute code just by carrying that one build file.' Aikido's own research is the second-source citation in the article. Hunting tier — node-gyp is benign for many native modules (sqlite3, sharp, bcrypt). The aggregation surfaces which native module a host is compiling so the SOC can baseline. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/npm-v12-block-postinstall
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059 T1027.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate native modules: sqlite3, better-sqlite3, sharp, bcrypt, canvas, node-sass, node-saml, node-pty — all use binding.gyp
  • CI builder building any Electron app from source
  • Native-module rebuild after a Node major version bump (common across the fleet at once)
  • Local 'npm install' on a developer laptop pulling in any C/C++-bound package
Suppression filter
| where NativeModule !in ("sqlite3","better-sqlite3","sharp","bcrypt","canvas","node-sass","sass","node-pty","node-saml","node-expat","deasync","fsevents","keytar","node-gyp","nodegit","grpc","@grpc/grpc-js")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull NativeModule from the aggregation. If it's in your known-good native-module allowlist (sqlite3, sharp, etc.) — close. If it's an unfamiliar package name, pivot npm registry view of that package and check publish date / maintainer change history. 2) CONTAIN: only escalate if the package is unknown — quarantine the host, snapshot the node_modules/<module>/build/ artifacts. 3) HUNT: pull the module's binding.gyp from disk and inspect 'actions' / 'sources' fields for shellouts. Search the fleet for that module name across DeviceProcessEvents to scope. Cross-ref against npm v12 readiness output ('npm approve-scripts --allow-scripts-pending').
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "node-gyp" and ProcessCommandLine has "rebuild")
    or ProcessCommandLine has "binding.gyp"
    or FileName in~ ("node-gyp.cmd","node-gyp.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe","npx.cmd","yarn.cmd","yarn.exe","pnpm.cmd","pnpm.exe","bun.exe")
    or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend NativeModule = extract(@"node_modules[\\/]+([^\\/]+)", 1, ProcessCommandLine)
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            Hits = count(),
            DistinctModules = dcount(NativeModule),
            SampleModules = make_set(NativeModule, 25),
            SampleCmd = any(ProcessCommandLine)
            by DeviceName, AccountName
| order by FirstSeen desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (CommandLine has "node-gyp" and CommandLine has "rebuild")
    or CommandLine has "binding.gyp"
    or NewProcessName has_any ("node-gyp.cmd","node-gyp.exe")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe","yarn.cmd","pnpm.cmd","bun.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend NativeModule = extract(@"node_modules[\\/]+([^\\/]+)", 1, CommandLine)
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Hits = count(),
            DistinctModules = dcount(NativeModule),
            SampleModules = make_set(NativeModule, 25),
            SampleCmd = any(CommandLine)
            by Computer, Account
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\node.exe OR *\\NODE.EXE OR *\\npm.exe OR *\\NPM.EXE OR *\\npm.cmd OR *\\yarn.cmd OR *\\pnpm.cmd OR *\\bun.exe) (@CommandLine:*node-gyp* OR @CommandLine:*binding.gyp*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^(node\.exe|npm\.(cmd|exe)|yarn\.(cmd|exe)|pnpm\.(cmd|exe)|bun\.exe)$/i CommandLine=/node-gyp.*rebuild|binding\.gyp/i
| regex("node_modules[\\\\/]+(?<native_module>[^\\\\/]+)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, native_module], function=count())
ENDPOINT

| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as sample_cmd from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node.exe","npm.exe","npm.cmd","npx.cmd","yarn.exe","yarn.cmd","pnpm.exe","pnpm.cmd","bun.exe")) AND (Processes.process="*node-gyp*rebuild*" OR Processes.process="*binding.gyp*" OR Processes.process_name IN ("node-gyp.cmd","node-gyp.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | rex field=sample_cmd "node_modules[\\\\/]+(?<native_module>[^\\\\/]+)" | stats min(firstTime) as firstTime max(lastTime) as lastTime values(native_module) as native_modules by dest user parent_process_name | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as sample_cmd from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node.exe","npm.exe","npm.cmd","npx.cmd","yarn.exe","yarn.cmd","pnpm.exe","pnpm.cmd","bun.exe")) AND (Processes.process="*node-gyp*rebuild*" OR Processes.process="*binding.gyp*" OR Processes.process_name IN ("node-gyp.cmd","node-gyp.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | rex field=sample_cmd "node_modules[\\\\/]+(?<native_module>[^\\\\/]+)" | stats min(firstTime) as firstTime max(lastTime) as lastTime values(native_module) as native_modules by dest user parent_process_name | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

title: Crypto-Wallet Keystore Access by Non-Wallet Process
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d02
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers / wallet drainers read keystore files from MetaMask,
    Exodus, Atomic, Phantom, Bitcoin, Electrum, Ethereum-cli wallets.
    Filtering out the legitimate wallet binaries leaves only attacker
    activity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1005/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1005
    - attack.collection
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Ethereum\keystore\'
            - '\Bitcoin\'
            - '\Exodus\'
            - '\Electrum\wallets\'
            - '\MetaMask\'
            - '\Phantom\'
            - '\Atomic\Local Storage\'
    filter_legit:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\MetaMask.exe'
            - '\Exodus.exe'
            - '\Atomic.exe'
            - '\electrum.exe'
            - '\Bitcoin.exe'
            - '\Phantom.exe'
    condition: selection_path and not filter_legit
falsepositives:
    - Backup software
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Ethereum\keystore\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Bitcoin\wallet.dat"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Exodus\exodus.wallet*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Electrum\wallets\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\MetaMask\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Phantom\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Atomic\Local Storage\*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Ethereum\keystore\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Bitcoin\wallet.dat"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Exodus\exodus.wallet*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Electrum\wallets\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\MetaMask\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Phantom\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Atomic\Local Storage\*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'

    filter_browser:

            - '\chrome.exe'

            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT

      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("142.11.206.73") or RemoteUrl has_any ("sfrclak.com", "webhook.site")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["142.11.206.73"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["sfrclak.com", "webhook.site"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: network_connection
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    selection_domain:
        DestinationHostname:
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    condition: selection_ip or selection_domain
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive IOC match
level: critical
NETWORK

    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("142.11.206.73")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("sfrclak.com", "webhook.site")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("sfrclak.com", "webhook.site")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("142.11.206.73")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("sfrclak.com", "webhook.site")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("sfrclak.com", "webhook.site")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]

Unauthenticated POST to meta-ads-mcp /mcp endpoint on TCP 8080 (CVE-2026-48039) AIExploitation High
Hunts for inbound HTTP POSTs to the /mcp endpoint on TCP 8080 that succeed without an Authorization header — the exact exploitation vector for CVE-2026-48039 where AuthInjectionMiddleware.dispatch() forwards unauthenticated requests to downstream MCP tool handlers. Correlates with successful 200 responses to confirm tool execution rather than rejection. Rationale: Article body explicitly names the /mcp endpoint, TCP 8080 default port, and POST verb in its PoC (docker run -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 ... POST /mcp HTTP/1.1). Combination of POST + /mcp + 8080 + 200 status + external source is the exploitation signature with near-zero benign baseline. No external sources cross-checked — advisory is the canonical source.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal monitoring/healthcheck POSTs from the same subnet (filter by src IP allow-list)
  • Authorized red-team or vulnerability scans against the MCP server
  • CI/CD integration tests hitting /mcp from a known build-runner IP
  • Authenticated MCP clients that don't strip the Authorization header but proxy strips it before logging
  • Internal misconfiguration where MCP is intentionally exposed to a trusted internal segment
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--host 127.0.0.1" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--host localhost" and RemoteIP !in (dynamic(["<known-monitoring-ip-1>","<known-scanner-ip-1>"]))
Response runbook
1. Triage: Pull the full request body and response for the matching session — confirm the JSON-RPC `tools/call` method invocation and inspect the response body for the substring `access_token=` in any `request_url` field (proof of token leakage). Identify the source IP, geo, and ASN; check threat-intel reputation. 2. Contain: Immediately block inbound 8080 from external networks at the perimeter firewall; if the meta-ads-mcp container is exposed (--host 0.0.0.0), restart with --host 127.0.0.1 binding or place behind an authenticated reverse proxy. Rotate the operator's META_ACCESS_TOKEN in Meta Business Manager and revoke any active sessions. 3. Hunt: Search outbound traffic from the host to graph.facebook.com for any URL containing `access_token=` (UC2); review Meta Ads activity log for unauthorized ad-account API calls during the exposure window; check for other exposed MCP servers in the estate via UC3.

Meta Graph API outbound URL leaking access_token in query string AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts for outbound HTTPS to graph.facebook.com with `access_token=` exposed as a URL query parameter — the api.py:136 vulnerability where meta-ads-mcp appends the operator token directly to the URL rather than using an Authorization header. Captured when proxy TLS inspection is enabled or via host-side process command-line / script-content telemetry. Both pre-error (every Graph call) and post-error (token echoed back to attacker) cases are covered. Rationale: Article shows the exact leakage shape: `request_url`: `https://graph.facebook.com/v24.0/me/adaccounts?...&access_token=FAKE_TOKEN_FOR_POC_DEMO_123456789`, and api.py:136 confirms the token is appended as a URL query param on every call. Detecting `graph.facebook.com` + `access_token=` in a URL is high-fidelity — Meta's documented best practice is Authorization header, so seeing the token in a URL is itself a misconfiguration signal.
ATT&CKT1041 T1552.001 T1528
Data sourcesWeb.Web Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy applications still using URL-based Graph API auth (Meta deprecated this pattern but it remains in some SDKs)
  • Developer/QA boxes running ad-hoc curl tests against Graph API
  • Marketing-automation tools that have not migrated to OAuth Bearer headers
  • Logging/observability pipelines that scrub URLs but echo the original in error messages
  • Proxy logs that capture the URL before redaction policies apply
Suppression filter
| where Url !has "client_id=" and Url !has "/oauth/access_token" and ActorUsername !in (dynamic(["<dev-test-account-1>","<known-marketing-svc>"]))
Response runbook
1. Triage: Extract the full URL and the captured `token_prefix`; cross-reference against the known operator token prefix (consult the Meta Business Manager admin to confirm which prefix maps to the production META_ACCESS_TOKEN). Identify the originating host and process. 2. Contain: Rotate the affected META_ACCESS_TOKEN immediately via Meta Business Manager — long-lived tokens are valid for 60 days. Audit any client of meta-ads-mcp that may have received the token in a JSON-RPC response. 3. Hunt: Search Meta Ads API audit logs (via Graph API `/me/business_users` activity) for actions performed by this token from non-corporate IPs in the last 30 days; look for spend manipulation, new ad-account permissions, or audience exports. Pivot to UC1 to find the unauthenticated /mcp POST that triggered the leak.

meta-ads-mcp listener bound to non-loopback interface (0.0.0.0:8080) AIInstallation High
Hunts for meta-ads-mcp processes that bind the HTTP MCP listener to a non-loopback interface (--host 0.0.0.0, --host *, or any non-127.0.0.1 address on port 8080) — the deployment-level misconfiguration that exposes the CVE-2026-48039 vulnerable endpoint to the network. Loopback-only bindings are out of scope; this catches the prerequisite for remote exploitation. Rationale: Article impact section states 'an unauthenticated attacker who can reach the MCP server's HTTP port (default 8080)' — the prerequisite is non-loopback exposure. PoC shows the safe loopback binding (`-p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080`) which intentionally limits exposure; we detect the opposite. Process-command-line pattern `meta_ads_mcp` + `--host 0.0.0.0` is article-grounded and high-fidelity.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Intentional deployment behind an authenticated reverse proxy where 0.0.0.0 binding is required for the proxy to reach the container (verify the proxy enforces auth)
  • Kubernetes pods where service mesh fronts the listener (binding is 0.0.0.0 but ingress is gated)
  • Internal lab/test deployments where exposure is bounded by network segmentation
  • Developer workstations running local dev containers (--host 0.0.0.0 is common but should not be allowed in production VLANs)
  • CI integration runners spinning up the server briefly for tests
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "--reverse-proxy" and DeviceName !in (dynamic(["<dev-workstation-1>","<ci-runner-1>"]))
Response runbook
1. Triage: Confirm the bind interface and port from the process command line; check `netstat -tlnp` / `ss -tlnp` (or `Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen`) to verify 8080 is actually listening on the public interface. Identify whether the host has a public IP or is behind a NAT/proxy. 2. Contain: Restart the meta-ads-mcp service with `--host 127.0.0.1` (loopback only) and place behind an authenticated reverse proxy (nginx + bearer-token auth, Traefik with forward-auth, or similar). Block inbound 8080 at the host firewall. 3. Hunt: Pivot to UC1 to check whether any external POST has already hit /mcp during the exposure window; pivot to UC2 to check whether the operator token has been seen in outbound URLs; check the version (UC4) to confirm whether the running build is in the ≤1.0.101 vulnerable range.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("meta_ads_mcp","meta-ads-mcp")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--host 0.0.0.0","--host *","--host 0","-h 0.0.0.0","HOST=0.0.0.0")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "--port 8080" and ProcessCommandLine !has "127.0.0.1" and ProcessCommandLine !has "localhost" and ProcessCommandLine !has "::1")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("meta_ads_mcp","meta-ads-mcp") or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("meta_ads_mcp","meta-ads-mcp")
| extend CmdLine = coalesce(TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessCommandLine)
| where CmdLine has_any ("--host 0.0.0.0","--host *","HOST=0.0.0.0","-h 0.0.0.0")
   or (CmdLine has "--port 8080" and CmdLine !has "127.0.0.1" and CmdLine !has "localhost")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, CmdLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable meta-ads-mcp version (<=1.0.108) inventory AIReconnaissance High
Identifies hosts running meta-ads-mcp in the vulnerable range (≤1.0.101 confirmed; 1.0.102–1.0.108 lack git tags and are unconfirmed-patch) via software inventory and process command-line version banners. Output feeds an asset-priority list for patching and feeds UC3 to flag the highest-risk hosts (vulnerable version + non-loopback binding). Rationale: Article explicitly states 'Affected version: ≤ 1.0.101' and 'vuln <= 1.0.108' in the package footer. Version regex `^1\.0\.([0-9]|[1-9][0-9]|10[0-8])$` matches the precise vulnerable range. Pulling from both TVM software inventory and live process command-lines gives both the dormant-install and actively-running signal — important because pip-installed packages can be present but not running.
ATT&CKT1518 T1592.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Versions 1.0.102–1.0.105 may be patched but cannot be confirmed without git tags — these will surface as potential vulnerable even if actually safe
  • Developer/CI hosts intentionally pinning an old version for regression testing
  • Vendored copies of meta-ads-mcp inside Docker base images where the image hasn't been rebuilt
  • Shadow IT installs where meta-ads-mcp was pulled into a venv outside the central inventory
  • Hosts with old `pip freeze` snapshots in inventory that no longer reflect current state
Response runbook
1. Triage: Cross-reference the output with UC3 to identify hosts that are both vulnerable AND exposed on a non-loopback interface — these are highest priority. Sort by LastSeen to find currently-running instances. 2. Contain: For exposed+vulnerable hosts, immediately apply the workaround (bind to 127.0.0.1 only, or block inbound 8080) and schedule emergency patching to ≥1.0.109 (next confirmed-fixed version per the advisory wording). 3. Hunt: For each vulnerable host, pull 90 days of UC1 (inbound /mcp POSTs) and UC2 (outbound graph.facebook.com URLs with access_token=) to establish whether exploitation has already occurred. Rotate META_ACCESS_TOKEN on any host where indicators are positive.
let VulnVersionRegex = @"^1\.0\.([0-9]|[1-9][0-9]|10[0-8])$";
let FromInventory = DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
  | where SoftwareName has_any ("meta-ads-mcp","meta_ads_mcp") or (SoftwareVendor =~ "pipeboard" and SoftwareName has "mcp")
  | where SoftwareVersion matches regex VulnVersionRegex
  | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, Source="TVM", SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion;
let FromProcess = DeviceProcessEvents

  | where isnotempty(SoftwareVersion) and SoftwareVersion matches regex VulnVersionRegex
  | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, Source="Process", SoftwareName="meta-ads-mcp", SoftwareVersion;

| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Sources=make_set(Source), Versions=make_set(SoftwareVersion) by DeviceId, DeviceName
| order by LastSeen desc

  • Vulnerability-management tool that runs the PoC for verification
  • Sandbox detonation environments analysing public exploit code
  • Documentation copies of the advisory committed to internal wiki / git that get scanned by EDR script-content collectors
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in (dynamic(["<authorized-redteam-account>","<vm-validation-svc>"])) and DeviceName !in (dynamic(["<sandbox-host-1>","<security-lab-1>"]))
Response runbook
1. Triage: Identify the source — is this an authorized red-team exercise (check change-management / RoE records) or an unsanctioned execution? Pull the parent process tree to determine if it was launched interactively or via remote execution. 2. Contain: If unsanctioned, isolate the host, terminate the docker/podman container, kill the Python process, and capture container/process memory for forensics. Block egress from the host pending review. 3. Hunt: From the same source IP / user account, search for UC1 hits (POST /mcp from this host's IP), UC2 hits (graph.facebook.com URLs with access_token=) in the prior 30 days, and any other hosts in the estate that received connections from this source — the PoC may have been used to scan internal MCP servers.
union
  (DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("meta-ads-mcp-vuln001","FAKE_TOKEN_FOR_POC_DEMO")
       or (ProcessCommandLine has "poc.py" and ProcessCommandLine has "/mcp")
       or (FileName in~ ("docker.exe","docker","podman.exe","podman") and ProcessCommandLine has "META_ACCESS_TOKEN" and ProcessCommandLine has "8080")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Source="Process", FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256),
  (DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName =~ "poc.py" and (FolderPath has "meta" or FolderPath has "mcp")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source="File", FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256)
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| extend Cmd = coalesce(TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessCommandLine)
| where Cmd has_any ("meta-ads-mcp-vuln001","FAKE_TOKEN_FOR_POC_DEMO")
   or (Cmd has "poc.py" and Cmd has "/mcp")
   or (Cmd has_any ("docker","podman") and Cmd has "META_ACCESS_TOKEN" and Cmd has "8080" and Cmd has "meta")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, Cmd, Hashes
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] FireAnt Metakit update process spawning script/LOLBin child (supply-chain payload exec)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — OceanLotus: From external espionage to domestic targeting
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SPECTRALVIPER sample hash sighting (file/process/module load) · [LLM] SPECTRALVIPER selective second-stage payload drop post-FireAnt update · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] OceanLotus SPECTRALVIPER C&C infrastructure callback (dated IOC set) · [LLM] OceanLotus Denis/SOUNDBITE DNS tunneling — high-entropy subdomains + TXT abuse · [LLM] OceanLotus PHOREAL ICMP covert C&C — sustained outbound ICMP with non-standard payloads · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains · DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
OceanLotus SPECTRALVIPER C&C infrastructure callback (dated IOC set) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to the specific SPECTRALVIPER C&C IPs and domains documented in the ESET 2024-2026 campaigns. Each IP/domain pair is dated in the article's IOC table, so first-seen dates can be cross-referenced to suspected first-compromise time. Rationale: Uses the dated C&C table (gatewayrvcenter.com→139.180.128.42 first-seen 2025-09-20, coachcybersecurity.com→139.99.33.239 2024-07-08, mxprodesign.com→166.88.77.186 2024-07-12, power-sync-services.com→103.119.47.104 2024-07-06) plus financemachinelearning.com (article body), and the article's IOC IP block. Cross-checked against MITRE G0050/APT32 page and Elastic Security Labs 2023 SPECTRALVIPER write-up which lists overlapping OceanLotus infrastructure conventions. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0050/ • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/elastic-charms-spectralviper
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel research VMs visiting known-bad domains during analysis
  • Sinkhole providers (CIRCL, Spamhaus) that have absorbed any of these domains
  • Generic VPS reuse — the IPs are on shared hosters (Vultr/OVH/Linode); a benign tenant could rotate onto an IP after OceanLotus moves off
  • Security tool scheduled IOC validation tasks pinging the indicators
  • Reverse DNS/PTR lookups by infrastructure monitoring tools
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","iexplore.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--type=utility","--headless") | where AccountName !endswith "$" and AccountName !in~ ("threatintel","soc-research")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256, command line and parent for the hitting connection — if it's a browser/legitimate tool the analyst may be researching; check that the user account isn't a known threat-intel researcher. Pivot on DeviceId across the last 90d to find prior connections to the broader OceanLotus IOC set. 2) Contain: isolate the device via Defender Live Response, block the IP/domain at perimeter and EDR network containment, force-rotate AAD tokens for the AccountName. 3) Hunt: search DeviceProcessEvents/DeviceFileEvents for the SPECTRALVIPER SHA1s on the same device, sweep your fleet for any of the 6 domains/8 IPs across the full retention window, and check if the host runs FireAnt Metakit (likely first-stage if so).

let SVIPER_DOMS = dynamic(["financemachinelearning.com","gatewayrvcenter.com","coachcybersecurity.com","mxprodesign.com","power-sync-services.com","leadingfilipinoteams.com"]);

SPECTRALVIPER sample hash sighting (file/process/module load) AIInstallation High
Matches the 20 SHA1s ESET attributes to SPECTRALVIPER samples observed in the FireAnt supply-chain and infrastructure-corporation campaigns. Any sighting in execution, file write, or DLL load telemetry is treated as confirmed OceanLotus presence. Rationale: Direct match against the 20 SHA1 hashes in the article's IOC block. Three telemetry views — process create, file write, image load — catch the binary regardless of whether it executes standalone, is dropped to disk, or is side-loaded as a DLL (OceanLotus's known DLL side-load TTP per MITRE G0050). Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0050/ • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/elastic-charms-spectralviper
ATT&CKT1059 T1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sandboxing/EDR/AV tools writing the sample for analysis on a research VM
  • VirusTotal/Hybrid-Analysis intel ingestion writing samples to disk in a research path
  • Honeypot detonation infrastructure
  • Backup of a previously infected machine being restored containing dormant copies of the binary
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !contains "\\Quarantine\\" and FolderPath !contains "\\Sandbox\\" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MpCmdRun.exe","SenseIR.exe","hybrid-analysis-collector.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree around the SHA1 sighting — Defender DeviceProcessEvents with ProcessId/ProcessCreationTime/InitiatingProcess* to identify how the binary got onto the host (FireAnt update? signed installer DLL side-load? scheduled task?). 2) Contain: EDR-isolate the host, quarantine the file by hash org-wide via Defender file blocking, force credential rotation for the AccountName and all logged-on users in the previous 30d (DeviceLogonEvents). 3) Hunt: sweep DeviceNetworkEvents on the same DeviceId for the C&C IPs/domains in UC1, check DeviceProcessEvents/DeviceFileEvents for FireAnt Metakit presence, and run UC4/UC5 against the same host to identify Denis (DNS) or PHOREAL (ICMP) auxiliary implants.
